a6552.speech: Welcomed this donation of food for the benefit of vulnerable people. He thanked all the donors under the guidance of the Ambassador of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in Ouagadougou.

a6737.speaker: Government of South Africa
a6737.name: Government of South Africa
a6737.speech: promised that it will not allow the withdrawal of some 427 million dollars in US support to harm its HIV programme.

a6737.speaker: Experts, cited by African News
a6737.name: Experts
a6737.title: cited by African News
a6737.speech: warn that the coming years could see hundreds of thousands of new infections.

a6737.speaker: African News
a6737.name: African News
a6737.speech: According to African News, South Africa has more people living with HIV than any other country in the world.

a6737.speaker: Patients interviewed by the South African press
a6737.name: Patients interviewed by the South African press
a6737.speech: say they were turned away at public hospitals ; Others say they were forced to buy HIV medicines on the black market, where the pills cost almost double the price.

a6737.speaker: South African authorities
a6737.name: South African authorities
a6737.speech: the authorities insist that this should not happen.

a6824.speaker: Leroy Victor, chairperson of the management committee, Walvis Bay municipality
a6824.name: Leroy Victor
a6824.title: chairperson of the management committee, Walvis Bay municipality
a6824.speech: Said the council is expecting to generate N$759 million while their expenditure is equal to their expected revenue: “No tariff adjustments on these services are proposed for the two consecutive financial years, despite the fact that service providers such as NamWater might increase their tariffs later this year. However, the council has managed to balance its operational budget as required.”

a6824.speaker: Leroy Victor, chairperson of the management committee, Walvis Bay municipality
a6824.name: Leroy Victor
a6824.title: chairperson of the management committee, Walvis Bay municipality
a6824.speech: Added residents should thus make use of the current amnesty meant to assist them in paying off their debt: “Amnesty interest will write off all outstanding interest levied once the capital amount has been settled in full and is in force until 31 December.”

a6824.speaker: Trevino Forbes, Walvis Bay mayor
a6824.name: Trevino Forbes
a6824.title: Walvis Bay mayor
a6824.speech: Earlier explained the initial debt in April this year stood at N$416 million with the council owing nothing to NamWater: “Considering the current outstanding service debt, I would humbly encourage our residents to keep on paying their utilities as this will provide the council with much needed revenue to execute its duties.” ; “We still ensured that the council pays its bills to our service providers. I think it is only fair for the public to also grant council the same courtesy by ensuring that they pay or make the necessary arrangements to settle their accounts.”

a6824.speaker: Trevino Forbes, Walvis Bay mayor
a6824.name: Trevino Forbes
a6824.title: Walvis Bay mayor
a6824.speech: Earlier attributed the high debt to the downward economic trajectory, Covid-19, unauthorised water reconnections and leakages among others.

a6832.speaker: Patrick Yaw Boamah, former Chairman of Ghana’s Parliamentary Finance Committee and MP for Okaikwei Central
a6832.name: Patrick Yaw Boamah
a6832.title: former Chairman of Ghana’s Parliamentary Finance Committee and MP for Okaikwei Central
a6832.speech: Has urged the nation to pivot from its reliance on imports and foreign aid toward a robust, self-sustaining industrial base; in a statement copied to GraphicOnline he underscored the urgent need to bolster local industries, particularly in pharmaceuticals, agro-processing, and textiles, to curb imports, boost exports, and fortify Ghana’s economy.

a6832.speaker: Patrick Yaw Boamah, former Chairman of Ghana’s Parliamentary Finance Committee and MP for Okaikwei Central
a6832.name: Patrick Yaw Boamah
a6832.title: former Chairman of Ghana’s Parliamentary Finance Committee and MP for Okaikwei Central
a6832.speech: While acknowledging the benefits of agoa, cautioned against viewing it as a long-term crutch: “An extension of agoa is welcome, but it cannot be indefinite,” he asserted. “We must wean ourselves from these policies and take deliberate steps to strengthen our own economic foundation.” ; “We cannot wait another twenty years, banking on agoa or external aid strategic thinking, real investment, and strong leadership are what will propel us forward.”

a6832.speaker: Patrick Yaw Boamah, former Chairman of Ghana’s Parliamentary Finance Committee and MP for Okaikwei Central
a6832.name: Patrick Yaw Boamah
a6832.title: former Chairman of Ghana’s Parliamentary Finance Committee and MP for Okaikwei Central
a6832.speech: Argued that Ghana’s economic aspirations—sustained growth, reduced unemployment, and global market relevance—hinge on the nation’s ability to produce rather than consume: “We cannot afford to sit back and be spoon-fed. The time for strategic action is now.”

a6832.speaker: Patrick Yaw Boamah, former Chairman of Ghana’s Parliamentary Finance Committee and MP for Okaikwei Central
a6832.name: Patrick Yaw Boamah
a6832.title: former Chairman of Ghana’s Parliamentary Finance Committee and MP for Okaikwei Central
a6832.speech: Defended the One District, One Factory programme, maintaining that such efforts are vital to building local capacity: “Without bold steps to industrialize, the job creation we’ve been promising will remain an illusion,” he warned.

a6832.speaker: Patrick Yaw Boamah, former Chairman of Ghana’s Parliamentary Finance Committee and MP for Okaikwei Central
a6832.name: Patrick Yaw Boamah
a6832.title: former Chairman of Ghana’s Parliamentary Finance Committee and MP for Okaikwei Central
a6832.speech: Highlighted several sectors ripe for investment: in pharmaceuticals he pointed to local companies like Tobinco, Ernest Chemist, and Kinapharma as candidates for greater support to produce medicines domestically, noted the textile industry holds untapped potential to generate significant revenue through exports, and urged the government to prioritise agribusiness as a cornerstone of economic diversification. He called for substantial financial commitments to these sectors: “If we want to compete in global markets with our crops and products, we must be prepared to invest heavily in their growth,” stressing that this demands not only funding but also strategic planning and unwavering political will.

a6890.speaker: World Bank paper “Aid and Resource Curse”
a6890.name: World Bank paper “Aid and Resource Curse”
a6890.speech: According to the paper, foreign aid can also be a factor in governments not carrying out reforms, in being spendthrift, in opting for financeable rather than priority projects, and in providing rents to political clienteles; another negative effect mentioned in the text is that project administration, with its high salaries, “subtracts” qualified staff from the State, weakening institutions.

a7021.speaker: Imani Mruma, Assistant Commissioner for Renewable Energy, Tanzanian Ministry of Energy
a7021.name: Imani Mruma
a7021.title: Assistant Commissioner for Renewable Energy, Tanzanian Ministry of Energy
a7021.speech: Said that so far only 10.5 megawatts of electricity from renewable sources enters the national grid, so the goal is to increase it; said various projects are being implemented, including the Kishapu solar project in Shinyanga region with capacity to generate 15 megawatts and a geothermal project in Songwe region that will produce 200 megawatts, and that other projects are at the feasibility study stage, including wind projects in Iringa, Njombe, Singida, Shinyanga and Kilimanjaro ; “We expect these projects altogether to produce 843 megawatts for us by 2028. We are at a good stage, and our goal by 2045 is to bring more than 1,000 megawatts into the national grid through the national plan for developing energy in the country.”

a7021.speaker: Dr James Mataragio, Deputy Permanent Secretary, Tanzanian Ministry of Energy
a7021.name: Dr James Mataragio
a7021.title: Deputy Permanent Secretary, Tanzanian Ministry of Energy
a7021.speech: Said the United States and India have made strides on the use of clean and renewable energy, while Tanzania is beginning that journey ; “There is a big campaign right now here in Tanzania on the use of clean cooking energy; as a country we are trying to push the implementation of that campaign, and that is why we are joining our colleagues from the United States and India, who have experience in this area, in order to train our young people.”

a7021.speaker: Manoj Verma, Deputy High Commissioner of the Indian High Commission in Tanzania
a7021.name: Manoj Verma
a7021.title: Deputy High Commissioner of the Indian High Commission in Tanzania
a7021.speech: Said they are confident that this development cooperation between the three countries will enable others to use India’s experience in the area of alternative energy, improving the lives of Tanzanians in a sustainable way.

a7021.speaker: Alexander Klaits, Acting Resident Director of USAID in Tanzania
a7021.name: Alexander Klaits
a7021.title: Acting Resident Director of USAID in Tanzania
a7021.speech: Said the cooperation will strengthen local capacity and increase business opportunities between American companies in Tanzania.

a7057.speaker: UN Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a7057.name: UN Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a7057.speech: Said there were over 30 humanitarian access impediments last month, undermining the floods response and forcing relief organizations to resort to more costly air and river transport. “Key access challenges included physical access constraints, violence against humanitarian personnel and assets, bureaucratic impediments and operational interference,” it said. Floods and highway insecurities across South Sudan in September 2024 worsened humanitarian access as 15 major supply routes were rendered impassable, impacting the delivery of essential humanitarian supplies to some 500,000 people, according to the agency.

a7057.speaker: UN Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a7057.name: UN Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a7057.speech: More than 890,000 people have been affected by flooding in 40 counties across South Sudan leading to massive displacement, loss of livelihoods and destruction of critical infrastructures, according to the UN humanitarian agency.

a7057.speaker: UN Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a7057.name: UN Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a7057.speech: Further underscored that the security situation along the Juba-Nimule Road, following an attack on a passenger bus, has posed a significant threat to the supply of essential goods to markets in Juba ; Stated that the abduction of humanitarian staff for ransom in Yei River County prompted MSF to suspend health services, leaving the population with reduced access to health care ; Said other incidents that impeded access along major roads include ambushes, robberies, harassment and theft reported in the Equatoria region and the Abyei Administrative Area.

a7057.speaker: UN Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a7057.name: UN Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a7057.speech: Points to bureaucratic impediments including multiple checkpoints along the Nile and the Sobat river, which it believes continue to impact access to humanitarian assistance; it also cites harassment of transport operators, interference with recruitment processes, boat seizures and the denial of access to quarrying sites in Malakal as factors delaying or increasing the cost of critical services.
